strengths: Novel and elegant idea: representing maps between shapes as the composition of invertible flow-matching models trained independently per shape into a shared Gaussian anchor distribution, enabling zero-shot correspondence without pairwise optimization or large-scale training data.

Representation-agnostic design: the same framework applies across meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric (tetrahedral) meshes, and even supports inter-representation matching (e.g., mesh-to-point-cloud), which is a clear practical advantage over most existing shape-matching pipelines tied to a specific discretization.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, KINECT) and against a wide range of baselines (KNN, OT, Functional Maps variants with ZoomOut/NAM refinement, NDP), plus a well-motivated ablation comparing embeddings (xyz vs WKS vs geodesic vs FMNet) and comparing FUSE's Flow Matching choice against a DDIM/diffusion-based alternative (GeomDist), which supports the specific design decisions made.

Interesting additional downstream demonstrations (human scan fitting/skinning, UV/mesh parametrization via texture transfer, volumetric correspondence) that showcase versatility beyond the core matching task and suggest broader utility of the representation.

The paper is generally clearly written, with a good conceptual figure (Fig. 1) and reasonably transparent description of the pipeline and its relation to prior work (GeomDist, Functional Maps, OT-based matching).
weaknesses: The method still fundamentally relies on a hand-crafted, task-specific feature embedding (e.g., small sets of geodesic landmark distances) to get good correspondence; as shown in the ablation, raw xyz coordinates fail entirely, meaning the touted 'representation-agnostic'/'zero-shot' claim is somewhat overstated since a suitable semantic embedding still needs to be engineered or learned per task, and its acquisition (e.g., landmark selection, geodesic computation on point clouds) is nontrivial for some modalities.

The paper acknowledges but does not adequately solve the smoothness/Dirichlet energy issue: FUSE consistently achieves worse (higher) Dirichlet energy than FMaps-based methods, attributed to the non-smooth nature of flow inversion from surface to distribution; this could limit downstream usefulness (e.g., texture transfer, UV mapping) where smooth maps matter, and the paper's mitigation (learning an MLP prior for UV, Section 5.3) is an ad hoc patch rather than a principled fix.

Point-cloud-only matching is explicitly flagged as a weak point (geodesics are unreliable on unstructured data), which undermines the claim of general cross-representation applicability; quantitative results (Table 3, KINECT) and Figure 6 show degraded accuracy in point-cloud settings relative to mesh/SDF cases.

Some quantitative claims are supported only by averaged aggregate tables (Table 3) without per-dataset breakdown or variance/statistical significance (e.g., over random seeds, multiple pair samples), making it hard to assess robustness; details on how many shape pairs, runtime cost, and computational overhead of training an independent flow per shape (which seems required for every new shape encountered) are not clearly quantified in the main text.

Efficiency claims ('computationally efficient') are asserted but not substantiated with runtime/memory comparisons against baselines (e.g., OT, Functional Maps, NDP) in the main paper; since a new flow model must apparently be trained per shape, scalability to large collections of shapes is unclear.

The additional application sections (human scan fitting, UV parametrization, volumetric correspondence) are presented briefly with limited quantitative evaluation (mostly qualitative figures, one small table for volumetric matching), so their contribution feels more like a demonstration of versatility than a rigorously validated set of applications.

Limitations and societal impact discussion is very brief (only a short paragraph in the conclusion), and does not discuss failure cases in depth (e.g., how badly FUSE fails under strong non-isometry beyond Dirichlet energy, or behavior with very sparse/noisy point clouds) despite these being flagged as issues.

strengths: Introduces a novel and conceptually elegant representation (FUSE) for maps between 3D shapes based on flow matching, using a shared Gaussian anchor distribution to bridge embedding spaces of a source and target shape, enabling zero-shot correspondence without pairwise optimization or large-scale training.

The representation is genuinely representation-agnostic: the paper demonstrates applicability across meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric (tetrahedral) meshes, as well as inter-representation matching, which is an advantage over pipelines tied to a specific discretization.

Strong experimental validation across four benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, KINECT) against a wide range of axiomatic and learned baselines (KNN, OT, FMaps and variants, NDP, ZoomOut, NAM), with FUSE achieving competitive or superior accuracy and notably higher coverage due to its invertibility-by-construction property.

Thoughtful ablations: comparison of embedding strategies (xyz, WKS, geodesic, FMNet) showing the flow's distributional-alignment effect, and comparison against the closely related diffusion-based GeomDist approach (DDIM) showing FUSE's deterministic FM inversion yields lower divergence and better map accuracy.

Demonstrates versatility beyond pure matching, with applications to human scan fitting/skinning via SMPL-X, mesh parametrization/UV mapping, and volumetric correspondence, showing the representation can serve as a general-purpose backbone, and can be used to initialize existing refinement methods (FUSE+ZO, FUSE+NAM).

Clear articulation of the method's relation to prior work (Flow Matching, Geometry Distributions), with a reasoned discussion of why FM's exact bidirectionality is preferable to diffusion-based approximate inversion for this task.
weaknesses: The method relies on a task-tailored pointwise embedding (e.g., geodesic distances to landmarks) that must already be reasonably informative for the flow to help; the paper notes the flow does not help when embeddings are already well-aligned or are not alignable at all, suggesting dependence on the quality of an externally supplied feature embedding.

The maps produced lack smoothness compared to FMaps-based methods, attributed to the non-smooth nature of flow inversion from surface to distribution; refinement strategies (ZO, NAM) mitigate but do not fully resolve this, and the root cause is not deeply analyzed.

Point-cloud-only matching is explicitly reported as a weak setting due to unreliable geodesic distance estimation on unstructured data, narrowing the claimed representation-agnostic generality for the purely point-cloud case.

Landmark-based geodesic embeddings require manual/semantic landmark selection, and sensitivity to landmark count/noise or fully automatic selection is not extensively analyzed, which somewhat limits insight into the robustness of the claimed zero-shot generality.

Some sections (e.g., SDF benchmark discussion, scan fitting, parametrization) are only qualitatively or partially quantitatively evaluated in the main paper, with deeper analysis deferred to supplementary material.
Computational cost/training time comparisons against baselines are not clearly reported despite the paper's claim of computational efficiency.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel idea: representing point-to-point maps between shapes as the composition of two invertible flow-matching models anchored to a shared Gaussian distribution. This is a fresh, theoretically grounded (via the CFM marginalization theorem) alternative to functional maps, optimal transport, and registration-based pipelines.

Representation-agnostic by design: the same pipeline works on meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric (tetrahedral) data, and even enables inter-representation correspondence (e.g., mesh-to-SDF), which is demonstrated concretely in Fig. 7 and Table 7 -- a capability not offered by most competing shape-matching frameworks.

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies: embedding choice (GFE vs. WKS vs. coordinates vs. learned features, Table 2), sensitivity to landmark perturbation and count (Fig. 4), FM vs. DDIM anchoring comparison with a quantitative KL/JS divergence analysis (Table 3, Fig. 11), anchor-distribution choice (Table 10), and solver/step-count cost-accuracy tradeoffs (Table 11). These substantially strengthen the empirical and conceptual case for design choices.

Broad evaluation across four standard benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, KINECT) plus new benchmarks the authors constructed for SDF and volumetric matching, with four complementary metrics (Euclidean, geodesic, Dirichlet, coverage) and full per-pair distribution plots in the supplement.

Demonstrates versatility beyond matching: human body scan fitting/re-posing via SMPL-X, UV/mesh parametrization by bijecting to a sphere, and volumetric correspondence, indicating the representation has value as a general-purpose "bridge" between geometric modalities.
Reasonable computational efficiency (per-shape training in ~2 minutes on a single GPU, <2GB memory), and inference cost is reported and compared to several baselines (Table 8).

Honest and specific discussion of limitations (symmetry disambiguation depends entirely on the embedding, degraded performance on point clouds due to unreliable geodesics, non-bijectivity of the final KNN step), which appropriately scopes the claims rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: The method is not consistently state-of-the-art: ULRSSM outperforms FUSE on FAUST and SMAL (Table 4), and FUSE's advantage is most pronounced specifically in the landmark-based, near-isometric setting; the paper's framing sometimes reads as more universally superior than the tables support.

The approach depends on manually chosen landmarks (5-6 per dataset) to build the Geodesic Feature Embedding, which is a supervision/prior requirement; while the authors justify this as standard in axiomatic pipelines, it somewhat undercuts claims of being training/prior free compared to fully unsupervised deep baselines.

Performance degrades notably on point clouds (KINECT, and point-cloud legs of the inter-representation experiments), where FUSE is often only second-best behind NDP, because it fundamentally relies on accurate geodesic distance estimation and uniform surface sampling -- both of which are unreliable on unstructured point clouds. This limits applicability to one of the most practically important input modalities.

The final correspondence step (nearest-neighbor search in embedding space) is explicitly non-bijective despite the invertibility of the flows, weakening one of the paper's central claimed advantages ("inherently enforcing bijectivity") -- the theoretical bijectivity guarantee does not carry through to the discrete matching output.

Each shape requires training its own independent flow network; although fast per shape, this is a per-instance optimization paradigm rather than an amortized/generalizable model, which may limit scalability to large-scale or streaming shape collections compared to feed-forward learned methods (e.g., ULRSSM, Diff3D) that pay training cost once.

The "curse of frequency" phenomenon (poor performance with high-frequency embeddings such as raw WKS) means the practical embedding choices that work well (GFE, smoothed WKS) are somewhat narrow, and the paper acknowledges the general integration of arbitrary learned embeddings with FUSE remains future work rather than a solved capability.

Some quantitative comparisons (e.g., SDF and volumetric benchmarks) are newly constructed by the authors without independent validation against established benchmarks, which, while a reasonable contribution given the lack of existing benchmarks, makes cross-paper comparability harder to assess.
